model: Life insurer FCFE at cost of equity, net debt held at zero (engine route)

inputs.sbc_source: FY2025 10-K cash flow statement add-back (MET_Metrics.csv StockBasedComp FY2025 $131M); MET publishes no combined equity-award-tax figure and award-settlement withholding is immaterial against a $2.9bn repurchase programme, so the add-back is used unadjusted
inputs.buyback_note: FY2025 repurchases of common stock $2,883M (financing line; FY2024 $3,207M, FY2023 $3,103M). H1-2026 $1,477M. A further $3bn authorisation was added with Q2-2026 results. Buybacks are the mechanism that keeps the count flat and are value-neutral in this model; the FCFE stream is what is capitalised.
inputs.share_count_basis: 635,477,000 common shares outstanding at July 31, 2026 (Q2-2026 10-Q cover) plus 4.3M incremental shares from stock-based awards (Q2-2026 EPS note, treasury-stock method) = 639.8M, rounded to 640.0M fully diluted; held FLAT because SBC is expensed in the flows (charged once). Weighted-average diluted count was 646.9M in Q2-2026 and 673.3M for FY2025; the count is falling ~4%/yr on repurchases, which this model does not credit as growth.
inputs.wacc_rationale: Cost of EQUITY 9.5% for a USD-denominated US life insurer: 10-year UST ~4.3% + 5.0% ERP x beta ~1.05, rounded. MetLife's own 2026 outlook assumes a 4.40% 10-year at December 2026. Higher than GL's 9.0% because MET carries more interest-rate, equity-market and credit sensitivity (spread-based RIS/PRT liabilities, variable annuity and long-term care run-off, 1.8x debt/equity). It is a cost of equity, not a WACC, because the flows are post-interest FCFE (holdco interest paid $903M in FY2025 is inside the adjusted-earnings margin). Same rate in all three scenarios; risk is carried in the driver paths and probability weights, not stacked into the discount rate.
inputs.lease_treatment: Not applicable: operating leases are immaterial for an insurer and are already inside the adjusted-earnings expense base; no lease adjustment in flows or bridge.
inputs.nci_treatment: Noncontrolling interests of $300M at 30 June 2026 (net income attributable to NCI $24M in FY2025) are deducted once, in the equity bridge at book value; the flows are built from consolidated adjusted earnings, which MET reports before NCI but the amount is immaterial (0.4% of adjusted earnings).
inputs.net_debt_treatment: Held at ZERO. Total debt at 30 June 2026 ~$20.1bn (long-term debt $14,467M at the FY2025 10-K carrying value, subordinated debt $5,144M and short-term debt $460M at 30 June 2026) is serviced inside the flows: holdco interest paid is a use of liquid assets inside MetLife's own free-cash-flow definition and interest expense on debt is inside adjusted earnings. Deducting it again after capitalising a post-interest stream would count it twice. The $19.3bn of consolidated cash is almost entirely general-account and subsidiary liquidity backing policy liabilities, not surplus; the $3.6bn of holding-company cash (31 Dec 2025) sits inside the $3.0-4.0bn buffer management treats as required, so none of it is added as surplus cash.
inputs.notes: MODEL: FCFE at cost of equity on a life insurer, run through the owner-FCF component engine with net debt at zero (the GL / IAG.AX / GMG.AX / CHC.AX cost-of-equity-stream precedent). The dcf-methods routing default for an insurer is BVPS-compounding x exit P/B; overridden because (1) GAAP equity is not a usable compounding base -- it fell from $74.6bn (FY2020) to $29.9bn (FY2022) on the LDTI restatement and the rate-driven AOCI swing (AOCI +$18.1bn at FY2020, -$22.6bn at FY2022, -$18.7bn at 30 June 2026) and it moves by billions a quarter with rates, and (2) MetLife does not compound book: it distributes essentially all holding-company free cash flow (FY2025 $4.4bn returned vs $4.9bn FCF) through dividends and repurchases, and management itself frames value creation as the free-cash-flow ratio (65-75% of adjusted earnings) and the ~$25bn of FCF targeted for 2025-2029. The value driver is therefore the holding companies' free cash flow, i.e. FCFE. ENGINE MAPPING: revenue = total revenues (premiums + policy fees + net investment income + other); ebitda_margin_path = pre-tax adjusted earnings BEFORE stock compensation as % of revenue, with the engine's 21% cash-tax rate reproducing MetLife's adjusted-earnings effective tax rate so that NOPAT = adjusted earnings before preferred dividends (FY2025: $6,137M = 7.96% of revenue; FY2024 $5,996M = 8.45%; H1-2026 $3,276M = 8.57%; base year-1 after-tax margin 8.2% x FY2026 revenue ~$79.7bn gives ~$6.5bn, i.e. ~$9.80 per weighted diluted share against the $9.75 consensus the Analysis cites); sbc_pct_path charges SBC (0.17% of revenue); da_pct_path = 0 (D&A immaterial; capex is not PP&E here); capex_pct_path = capital RETAINED in the insurance subsidiaries (statutory new-business strain, RBC/local capital growth, subsidiary capital contributions and holdco expenses), calibrated so the base-case FCFE to common runs at ~72-73% of adjusted earnings available to common -- inside management's 65-75% two-year-average target and consistent with ~$25bn of FCF over 2025-2029 against ~$34bn of cumulative adjusted earnings, and below the 79-82% actually delivered in FY2024-25 (which included $437M of leverage-neutral debt issuance in FY2025 and ran above target); bull 75-78% (FY2024-25 run-rate sustained), bear 65% (bottom of target); cash_tax_rate_path flat at 21% (adjusted-earnings effective rate; GAAP cash taxes paid were $1,564M in FY2025). PREFERRED STOCK: the flows are BEFORE preferred dividends (adjusted earnings, not adjusted earnings available to common) and the $2,905M liquidation preference of the perpetual preferred (after the $1bn Series redemption in Q3-2025; FY2026 dividend run-rate ~$150M) is deducted once in the equity bridge at liquidation value, which is more conservative than capitalising the ~5.2% coupons at the 9.5% cost of equity. last_fcf = FY2025 free cash flow of all holding companies ($4,890M, MetLife's own definition, after preferred dividends) plus the $194M preferred dividends = $5,084M before preferred, matching the flow basis; reported_fcf = the company-defined $4,890M. An insurer's OCF-less-capex (FY2025 OCF $17,092M) is not free cash, so the owner-FCF identity last_fcf = reported_fcf - sbc - interest_income is deliberately not satisfied here. BVPS cross-check: GAAP book value per common share ~$38 (27,441 - 2,905 preferred over 640M), ~$68 ex-AOCI; MetLife's own adjusted BVPS (ex-AOCI other than FCTA) runs in the high-$50s, so the $94 price is ~1.6x adjusted book against a 15-17% adjusted ROE target -- a cross-check that supports, rather than drives, the FCFE answer.

equity_bridge.item: Preferred stock at liquidation preference (Series A, D, E, F, G; perpetual, non-cumulative)
equity_bridge.note: FY2025 10-K; $1bn redeemed Q3-2025; flows are before preferred dividends so the claim is deducted once here
Q2-2026 10-Q balance sheet; flows are consolidated adjusted earnings before NCI

historical_growth.growth_rate_source: Base-case ten-year average revenue growth: 3.4% in FY2026 (consensus ~$79.7bn, H1-2026 +6.5% YoY on PRT and Japan), 4.0% in FY2027-28 as adjusted PFOs ex-PRT grow ~5% and net investment income compounds with general-account assets, decelerating to the 2.5% terminal rate; brackets the 2.6-3.9% historical revenue CAGRs
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: GAAP equity and GAAP EPS CAGRs are meaningless for MET: the LDTI adoption and the rate-driven AOCI swing took reported equity from $74.6bn (FY2020) to $29.9bn (FY2022), so the 5yr equity CAGR of -17.5% diverges from revenue (+2.6%) by far more than 30%. GAAP EPS (-3.7%/-9.3%) is dominated by derivative and market-risk-benefit marks (FY2025 net income $3.4bn vs adjusted earnings $6.1bn). Growth was selected from revenue history, adjusted PFO growth and management's outlook, not from equity or EPS.
historical_growth.notes: fcf_3yr_cagr and fcf_5yr_cagr are on cash returned to common shareholders (dividends + repurchases: FY2020 $2,808M, FY2022 $4,924M, FY2025 $4,392M) as the only consistently disclosed proxy for distributable FCFE across the window; both are distorted (FY2020 buybacks were paused for COVID, FY2025 capital was diverted to the $1bn preferred redemption and the PineBridge acquisition). MetLife's own holding-company free cash flow was $4,890M in FY2025 and $4,559M in FY2024 (10-K liquidity section); adjusted earnings available to common grew $5.5bn (FY2023) -> $5,796M (FY2024) -> $5,943M (FY2025), a 2yr CAGR of 3.95%, and H1-2026 was $3.2bn vs $2.7bn (+18%). Reported FCF (OCF $17.1bn) is an insurer's operating cash flow and was not used for any CAGR.

base.narrative: Revenue +3.4% in FY2026 then 4% as group benefits and RIS grow adjusted PFOs ~5% ex-PRT and net investment income compounds with the general account, decelerating to 2.5%; pre-tax pre-SBC adjusted margin drifts from 10.55% (after-tax 8.2%, between FY2025's 7.96% and H1-2026's 8.57%) to 10.95% (after-tax ~8.5%) as the direct expense ratio falls from 12.1% toward 11.3% in 2029 and MIM scales, partly offset by group-benefits pricing competition and variable-investment-income normalisation; capital retention held at 2.2% of revenue (FCFE ~72-73% of adjusted earnings to common, inside the 65-75% target); tax 21%; terminal at min(Gordon 9.5%/2.5%, 14x FCFE).

bull.narrative: New Frontier keeps running ahead of plan: group benefits compounds mid-to-high single digits on voluntary/pet/legal adjacencies, Chariot Re and PRT flow lift RIS, MIM passes $1 trillion AUM with PineBridge, Asia and Latin America grow double digits in local currency, rates hold near 4.4% so spread income and variable investment income run at or above plan, and the expense ratio reaches 11.3% early; after-tax margin reaches ~9.0% and the FCF ratio stays at the 75-78% delivered in FY2024-25; terminal growth 3.0%, cap 16x (Gordon binds).

bear.narrative: A rate downcycle and recession: the 10-year falls back toward 3%, compressing RIS/PRT spreads and variable investment income, PRT pricing is competed away by reinsurers and new entrants, group-benefits sales slow with employment and disability incidence rises, a long-term-care reserve strengthening and VA hedge costs land in Corporate & Other, FX (yen, peso) translates earnings lower, and private-credit losses lift the cost of risk; after-tax margin falls from 7.7% to ~7.1%, regulators keep more capital in the subsidiaries so the FCF ratio sits at 65% (bottom of target), revenue grows ~2%; terminal growth 2.0%, cap 11x.

scenario_narratives.base: MetLife does roughly what its five-year plan says: low-to-mid single-digit revenue growth, an after-tax adjusted margin that edges from ~8.2% to ~8.5% on expense discipline and asset-management scale, and about 72-73% of adjusted earnings to common converted into holding-company free cash flow and returned through dividends and repurchases. Value is the FCFE stream at a 9.5% cost of equity, less the preferred stock at liquidation; GAAP book value, which swings with rates, is a cross-check only. The axes that matter are the level of long rates (spread income, variable investment income), group-benefits underwriting and pricing, PRT and Chariot Re flow, MIM scaling and the expense-ratio glide path, and the legacy long-term care and variable annuity blocks.
scenario_narratives.bull: New Frontier delivers on every pillar at once: group benefits leadership and adjacencies, retirement-platform growth with third-party capital, MIM past $1 trillion AUM, and faster Asia/LatAm growth, in a rate environment that keeps spread and variable investment income full. The after-tax margin reaches ~9% and the FCF ratio stays at the 75-78% delivered in FY2024-25. Even then the exit is capped at 16x FCFE: MetLife is a mature, leveraged life insurer, not a growth compounder.
scenario_narratives.bear: The structural sensitivity the Analysis flags as high severity -- long rates and the legacy LTC/VA blocks -- turns against the company. A rate downcycle compresses spread income and variable investment income, PRT pricing is competed away, a recession slows group-benefits sales and lifts disability claims, LTC reserve strengthening and hedge costs recur, FX and private-credit losses add up, and regulators keep more capital in the subsidiaries. Earnings stall, the FCF ratio sits at the bottom of the 65-75% range, and the stock de-rates to a low-double-digit FCFE multiple.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Bear raised from the 15% house default to 25%: the Analysis rates interest-rate sensitivity and the legacy long-term care block as high-severity risks, debt/equity is ~1.8x, and a leveraged spread-based balance sheet has asymmetric downside in a rate-and-credit downcycle. Bull cut from 35% to 25% because it needs several independent things to hold at once -- rates staying near 4.4%, PRT and Chariot Re flow, MIM scaling, the full expense-ratio glide and the FY2024-25 FCF ratio persisting above management's own 65-75% target. Base 50%: the plan is running ahead of schedule (Q2-2026 adjusted ROE 17%, adjusted EPS +20%) and the base case already credits that.

valuation_philosophy.summary: MetLife is valued as the present value of the free cash flow its holding companies can actually extract -- dividends and returns of capital from the insurance and asset-management subsidiaries after statutory capital retention, holding-company interest and expenses -- discounted at a 9.5% cost of equity over a ten-year explicit horizon, with the perpetual preferred stock deducted at its $2.9bn liquidation preference and no separate net-debt deduction because the ~$20bn of holdco debt is serviced inside the flows. The flow is calibrated to MetLife's own disclosed free cash flow ($4.9bn FY2025, $4.6bn FY2024; 65-75% two-year-average target; ~$25bn planned for 2025-2029), not to GAAP operating cash flow or GAAP book value, both of which are meaningless for a life insurer under LDTI. The terminal value is capped at 14x FCFE in base (11x bear, 16x bull). Buybacks are not credited as growth: the share count is held flat at 640M and the double-digit adjusted EPS growth management targets is, in this model, mostly the FCFE being returned rather than value created.
key_risks_to_valuation: Capital-retention assumption (capex_pct 2.2% of revenue in base, i.e. FCFE ~72-73% of adjusted earnings to common) is the single most important driver: every 10pp of FCF ratio is worth roughly $12-15/share; it is calibrated to management's 65-75% target and the ~$25bn 2025-29 plan, below the 79-82% delivered in FY2024-25

Interest rates: the base assumes the 10-year holds near 4.4% as in management's outlook; a sustained move toward 3% compresses RIS/PRT spreads and variable investment income (the bear case) and the $18.7bn AOCI unrealised-loss position would reverse, but AOCI does not affect the FCFE stream unless bonds are sold

Legacy long-term care and variable annuity blocks in Corporate & Other: a reserve strengthening or hedge-cost spike lands directly in adjusted earnings and is modelled only in the bear case beyond the ~$290M/yr Corporate & Other drag inside the base margin
Adjusted earnings include ~$1.6bn (pre-tax) of assumed variable investment income in 2026; private equity returns below the 9% assumption push the after-tax margin below the 8.2% base year-1 level

Group benefits (28% of adjusted earnings) is a commoditised renewal market; a pricing cycle or adverse mortality/morbidity moves the margin by tens of basis points, which is material on a ~8% after-tax margin
FX translation of Japan, Mexico and Chile earnings (Asia + LatAm = 41% of FY2025 adjusted earnings) and emerging-market regulatory risk

Revenue is lumpy (jumbo pension risk transfers book as premiums: FY2025 +8.6%); the margin-on-revenue construction means a PRT-heavy year inflates revenue and dilutes the margin without changing FCFE, so year-to-year comparisons of the driver paths should be made on adjusted earnings, not revenue
